title: The Potential Economic Costs of Quebec Independence: A Scenario-Based Assessment
content: Quebec’s sovereignty aspirations raise questions about the economic consequences of reorganizing established relationships within the Canadian federation, specifically with English, Inuit, and Indigenous nations. This study assesses potential GDP shortfalls, employment exposure, and unemployment under alternative independence scenarios. Using official 2024 economic and labour-force data and price-adjusted provincial input-output multipliers, the analysis models three illustrative trade and investment shocks alongside separately imposed 10% and 15% GDP reduction benchmarks. Annual GDP shortfalls range from CAD 3.82 billion to CAD 30.07 billion across the trade and investment scenarios, equivalent to 0.62%–4.88% of baseline GDP, with approximately 30,500–239,700 exposed jobs. The 10% and 15% benchmarks yield shortfalls of CAD 61.68 billion and CAD 92.52 billion and conditional employment equivalents of approximately 491,600 and 737,400 jobs. Assuming half of exposed positions translate into additional unemployed persons, unemployment reaches 10.42% and 12.97%, respectively. A separate northern territorial scenario distinguishes GDP reassignment from production losses, using Nord-du-Québec as an accounting proxy rather than delineating Cree and Inuit territories. Political violence and political instability are not quantified because suitable comparative data and a validated model are unavailable. These conditional estimates highlight the importance of trade continuity, labour-market adjustment, legal and negotiated arrangements, and the need to preserve culture, language, identity, and self-determination beyond economic measures.
